messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi was twenty years old, a writer from a tight-knit South Asian family in New Jersey, when his older brother Arjun died instantly in a hit-and-run on the highway. Ravi had been the one to receive the call—a stranger’s voice, a hospital name he didn’t recognize—and the memory of that phone still came back in fragments: the way his hand shook, the silence that followed, the slow realization that nothing would ever be the same. He had always believed the world was fundamentally fair, that hard work and love kept people safe. That belief had been destroyed in a single sentence over the phone. Now, six months later, he described himself as someone who used to be happy but was now permanently miserable, and he could not shake the conviction that the world was a dangerous place where any ordinary moment could turn catastrophic.

The danger felt real, not abstract. Ravi found himself unable to relax even in his own apartment, a space he had once considered his sanctuary. Ordinary sounds—the hum of the refrigerator, the creak of floorboards, the clatter of a neighbor’s keys—made him jump, his heart lurching as if a car were about to crash through the wall. Sleeping had become a nightly ordeal; he lay awake for hours, ears straining into the dark, waiting for the phone to ring again. These threat reactions, he came to believe, were necessary vigilance. If he let his guard down, something terrible would happen again. His negative appraisals of the world as unsafe directly fed his constant sense of threat, and that threat, in turn, reinforced his view that the world could never be trusted.

To manage this overwhelming state, Ravi had developed a set of strategies that seemed protective but only deepened his isolation. He stopped making any plans beyond the next few hours—no weekend trips, no freelance deadlines, no thoughts about his future as a writer. When his friends invited him to a café where he and Arjun used to write together, he refused without explanation, avoiding any reminder of his brother. He also caught himself repeatedly asking his mother, “Am I going to be okay?” and “Is it normal to feel this way?”—seeking reassurance that he was not losing his mind. These maladaptive strategies were directly shaped by his shattered beliefs: if the world was dangerous and his happiness was gone forever, then planning ahead felt pointless and reminders were unbearable. His avoidance of grief reminders and future plans reinforced his negative appraisals because every time he turned down an invitation or refused to think about tomorrow, he confirmed to himself that his life was permanently broken. The cycle tightened when his avoidance also fed his threat system: by retreating from any potential triggers, he never learned that he could survive them, so his startle response and hypervigilance only grew worse.

Ravi’s work as a writer suffered. He used to draft short stories in coffee shops, but now he could not sit still in any public space; the scrape of a chair or the sizzle of an espresso machine sent him scanning the room for danger. He worked only from his bedroom, and even there the page stayed blank. His editor had stopped asking about deadlines. His relationships also frayed—his friends, tired of his repeated requests for reassurance and his refusal to meet, began calling less often. He noticed the distance but told himself it was just another proof that the world was cold and that he was unworthy of connection.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a night when he tried to write a single sentence about a brother in a story and found himself on the floor, gasping, convinced he was about to die. He realized he could not go on like this. He was terrified that talking about Arjun would make the pain worse, and he was equally afraid that if he did not talk, he would lose every part of himself that still existed. In the waiting room of the clinic, he held a folded paper with Arjun’s name on it and wondered if he would ever again be able to make a plan that stretched beyond the next hour.
